POLAR: Online Learning for LoRA Adapter Caching and Routing in Edge LLM Serving

Shaoang Li Affiliation: Stony Brook University email: shaoang.li@stonybrook.edu and Jian Li Affiliation: Stony Brook University email: jian.li.3@stonybrook.edu
© none
Abstract.

Edge deployment of large language models (LLMs) increasingly relies on libraries of lightweight LoRA adapters, yet GPU/DRAM can keep only a small resident subset at a time. Serving a request through a non-resident adapter requires paging its weights from storage, incurring measurable latency. This creates a two-timescale online control problem: on a slow timescale, the system selects which adapters remain resident in fast memory, while on a fast timescale it routes each request to an adapter whose context-dependent utility is unknown a priori. The two decisions are tightly coupled: the cache determines the cost of exploration, and the router determines which adapters receive informative feedback. We formulate this joint caching-and-routing problem as a two-timescale contextual bandit and propose POLAR (Paging and Online Learning for Adapter Routing). POLAR pairs a cache-aware LinUCB router with an epoch-based cache controller. We study two variants. A fixed-epoch version provides a robust baseline with worst-case regret guarantees under arbitrary contexts. An epoch-doubling version, POLAR+, adds forced exploration and improved cache optimization to achieve 𝒪~​(d​N​T+K​T)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(d\sqrt{NT}+\sqrt{KT}) sublinear regret under stochastic regularity and cacheability conditions, where NN is the adapter count, KK the cache size, dd the context dimension, and TT the horizon. The routing term matches the standard contextual-bandit rate up to logarithmic factors, showing that the memory hierarchy does not fundamentally slow routing learning. Experiments using 15 real LoRA adapters for Qwen2.5-7B together with measured GPU paging latencies show that adaptive cache control substantially outperforms non-adaptive baselines and exhibits scaling trends consistent with the theory.

1. Introduction

Edge deployment of large language models (LLMs) is increasingly moving toward a modular design: a single base model is kept on device, while many downstream functionalities are implemented through lightweight adapters such as LoRA modules (Hu et al., 2022). This architecture is attractive because it avoids replicating the full base model for every task or tenant, and makes it practical to support diverse behaviors including translation, summarization, recommendation, code generation, and domain-specific assistance on resource-constrained edge servers. However, this modularity introduces a systems bottleneck that is easy to overlook: while the adapter library may contain tens or hundreds of specialized adapters, GPU/DRAM can hold only a small subset at any time. The rest remain on local storage and can be accessed only through a slower path that incurs nontrivial loading delay (Sheng et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2025; Li et al., 2024).

This memory-hierarchy constraint makes adapter residency a first-order systems decision rather than a mere implementation detail. In an interactive edge service, routing a request to a resident adapter yields a low-latency hot execution path, whereas routing it to a non-resident adapter requires a cold path, e.g., loading weights from SSD or flash into fast memory, which can substantially increase time-to-first-token and tail latency. Existing systems work has shown that LoRA loading and memory management are critical to end-to-end serving efficiency, but the missing online decision is which adapters should remain resident in fast memory in the first place. That decision is inherently dynamic: the most valuable resident set depends on the request stream, and that value is not known in advance.

This yields a natural two-timescale architecture. On a slow timescale, the system control plane selects a resident working set of at most KK adapters to keep in GPU/DRAM. Frequent reconfiguration is undesirable because loading new adapters incurs overhead and can destabilize service, so the resident set should change only periodically. On a fast timescale, the data plane routes each incoming request to an adapter. Crucially, the request need not be restricted to the current resident set: a non-resident adapter may still be the best choice for the query, but selecting it incurs an additional latency penalty. The resulting problem is therefore neither standard caching nor standard routing. The cache determines which adapters are cheap to access, while routing determines which adapters are used and thus which ones generate informative feedback for future decisions.

The challenge is amplified by uncertainty. Adapter quality is request-dependent and typically unknown a priori: an adapter that performs well on one class of queries may be poor on another. Hence the system must learn, online, how adapter utility varies with context while simultaneously managing a scarce memory resource. This creates an endogenous feedback loop. If the resident set is poorly chosen, potentially useful adapters remain expensive to probe, slowing learning. If routing is shortsighted, the system may collect feedback only on currently cheap adapters and fail to discover better ones. In other words, the value of caching an adapter is not exogenous; it depends on the future routing policy, which itself depends on what has been learned so far.

This raises the central question of the paper:

This coupled control problem differs fundamentally from prior work in adjacent areas. If all adapters were equally accessible, it would reduce to contextual model selection. If adapter quality were known ahead of time, it would reduce to cache management with fixed values; and if the resident set could be changed on every request without cost, it would collapse to a one-timescale paging model. None of these abstractions captures practical edge LLM serving. Existing systems such as S-LoRA (Sheng et al., 2023), FastLibra (Zhang et al., 2025), and EdgeLoRA (Shen et al., 2025) optimize adapter loading and memory sharing, but do not study the online decision problem of jointly learning adapter utility and managing residency under request-dependent performance.

We study this problem through the lens of edge LLM serving and formulate it as a two-timescale online learning problem. The system hosts a fixed base LLM and a library of adapters on storage. Time is divided into epochs. At each epoch boundary, the controller selects a resident set of size at most KK. During the epoch, each request arrives with a context vector, and the router selects an adapter from the full library. If the selected adapter is resident, the request follows the hot path; otherwise, it is served through the cold path and pays an additional latency penalty. We focus on the practically important regime in which the workload is approximately stable over the timescale of cache reconfiguration, so the target operating point is a steady resident set rather than continual cache churn. In this setting, the core online task is to learn which adapters deserve residency while still making good request-level routing decisions.

To address this challenge, we propose POLAR (Paging and Online Learning for Adapter Routing), a framework that mirrors the system hierarchy (Figure 1). POLAR combines a fast-timescale cache-aware LinUCB router with a slow-timescale cache controller that updates the resident set only at epoch boundaries. We study two variants. The first, POLAR, uses fixed-length epochs and greedy cache updates, and serves as a robust baseline that applies under arbitrary context sequences. The second, POLAR+, augments this design with forced exploration, exact cache optimization, and geometrically increasing epochs. The role of POLAR+ is not merely to improve constants: it overcomes the persistent cache-identification difficulty that remains in the unrestricted setting, and under additional workload regularity and cacheability conditions it achieves sublinear regret.

The analysis reveals a technical obstacle that does not arise in either standard contextual bandits or standard online caching. In ordinary contextual bandits, uncertainty about an arm depends on how often that arm is sampled. Here, sampling itself is shaped by the memory hierarchy: resident adapters are cheaper to explore, while non-resident adapters are more expensive, so the cache changes the data-collection process. As a result, the slow-timescale cache decision is statistically coupled with the fast-timescale learner. Our results show that this coupling can nevertheless be controlled. For the fixed-epoch variant, we establish a worst-case regret guarantee under the linear contextual model, and show that the resulting linear cache gap is intrinsic under arbitrary contexts rather than an artifact of the proof. For POLAR+, we show that under stationary workload regularity and a natural cacheability condition, epoch doubling and forced exploration make the cumulative cache-identification error summable, yielding an overall sublinear regret bound. The routing term matches the standard contextual-bandit rate up to logarithmic factors, showing that the memory hierarchy does not fundamentally slow routing learning. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first such guarantee for joint adapter caching and contextual routing in edge LLM serving.

Our contributions are summarized as follows.

  • •

    We formulate edge LoRA serving as a two-timescale online control problem over a memory hierarchy, coupling slow resident-set selection with fast contextual routing under hot/cold latency asymmetry.

  • •

    We propose POLAR and POLAR+, two two-timescale algorithms for joint adapter routing and cache placement. POLAR is a robust baseline under arbitrary contexts, while POLAR+ adds epoch doubling, forced exploration, and improved cache optimization to obtain provably sublinear regret under additional structure.

  • •

    We prove a worst-case regret bound for POLAR and show that its linear cache gap is intrinsic without workload regularity. We further prove a sublinear regret bound for POLAR+ under stochastic regularity and cacheable diversity, with a routing term matching the standard contextual-bandit rate up to logarithmic factors.

  • •

    We evaluate the proposed methods using real LoRA adapters on Qwen2.5-7B together with measured GPU paging latencies. The results show that adaptive cache control substantially reduces regret relative to non-adaptive baselines and exhibits scaling trends consistent with the theory.

2. System Model

We consider an edge device hosting a fixed base LLM and a library of NN lightweight adapters (e.g., LoRA modules), indexed by ℳ={1,…,N}\mathcal{M}=\{1,\dots,N\}. The full library resides on local storage, while only 1≤K≪N1\leq K\ll N adapters can be kept resident in fast memory (GPU/DRAM). A non-resident adapter can still serve a request through a slower path, e.g., paging from storage into fast memory, incurring an additional latency penalty.

Time is slotted into rounds t=1,…,Tt=1,\dots,T, grouped into epochs ℓ=1,2,…\ell=1,2,\dots. At each round, the system observes a context xt∈ℝdx_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} with ‖xt‖2≤1\|x_{t}\|_{2}\leq 1. The problem operates on two timescales. On a slow timescale, the resident set Cℓ⊆ℳC_{\ell}\subseteq\mathcal{M} with |Cℓ|≤K|C_{\ell}|\leq K is chosen at epoch boundaries and remains fixed during the epoch. On a fast timescale, the system selects an adapter at∈ℳa_{t}\in\mathcal{M} for each request, incurring low latency if at∈Cℓ⁡(t)a_{t}\in C_{\ell(t)} (hot), where ℓ⁡(t)\ell(t) denotes the epoch containing round tt, and an additional latency penalty otherwise (cold). This two-timescale abstraction reflects practical edge serving stacks, where cache reconfiguration is a slower control-plane operation, while request routing is a fast data-plane decision.

Each adapter aa has an unknown parameter θa⋆∈ℝd\theta_{a}^{\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} with ‖θa⋆‖2≤1\|\theta_{a}^{\star}\|_{2}\leq 1, and a known cold-path penalty λa>0\lambda_{a}>0, which captures the additional latency of serving a request through a non-resident adapter. This penalty depends on the adapter and the memory/storage hierarchy, and is assumed measurable by profiling before deployment. The context xtx_{t} encodes request features such as task type, input length, or domain, and θa⋆\theta_{a}^{\star} captures how adapter aa responds to these features. The observed quality is

where α>0\alpha>0 trades off service quality against latency. Thus, routing to a cold adapter is allowed, but pays an explicit penalty.

We model this by a switching cost γ​|Cℓ∖Cℓ−1|\gamma|C_{\ell}\setminus C_{\ell-1}| with γ>0\gamma>0, which reflects the one-time cost of loading each newly admitted adapter into the cache at epoch boundaries. An online policy selects {at}\{a_{t}\} and {Cℓ}\{C_{\ell}\} to maximize

Benchmark and regret. Define the noiseless reward

(4) μt(a;C):=⟨θa⋆,xt⟩−αλa𝟏{a∉C}.\displaystyle\mu_{t}(a;C):=\langle\theta_{a}^{\star},x_{t}\rangle-\alpha\lambda_{a}\mathbf{1}\{a\notin C\}.

We benchmark against a fixed resident set for two reasons. First, frequent cache reconfiguration is costly and undesirable in practical edge systems, so the target operating point is typically a stable working set rather than continual cache churn. Second, in the approximately stationary regime, a fixed cache provides the appropriate steady-state benchmark: the online problem is not to track arbitrary drift, but to learn which adapters deserve residency while paying routing exploration and occasional reconfiguration costs.

3. Algorithms

We present two variants of POLAR (Paging and Online Learning for Adapter Routing). Both follow the same two-timescale design. On the fast timescale, a cache-aware LinUCB router selects an adapter for each request. On the slow timescale, a cache controller updates the resident set only at epoch boundaries. The key difference between the two variants is how the resident set is updated and how exploration is enforced.

3.1. POLAR: A Fixed-Epoch Baseline

We begin with a simple and practical baseline, POLAR (Algorithm 1), which uses fixed-length epochs of HH rounds. Within each epoch, the resident set remains fixed, and the router computes for every adapter a cache-aware upper-confidence score

(8) scoret(a)=⟨θ^a,xt⟩+βtxt⊤​Va−1​xt−αλa𝟏{a∉Cℓ}.\displaystyle\mathrm{score}_{t}(a)=\langle\hat{\theta}_{a},x_{t}\rangle+\beta_{t}\sqrt{x_{t}^{\top}V_{a}^{-1}x_{t}}-\alpha\lambda_{a}\mathbf{1}\{a\notin C_{\ell}\}.

The first two terms are the standard LinUCB estimate and uncertainty bonus, where θ^a\hat{\theta}_{a} and VaV_{a} are the ridge estimate and regularized design matrix maintained by the algorithm (explicit form in Section 4) and βt\beta_{t} is the confidence radius specified in Lemma C.1; the last term explicitly penalizes routing through the cold path. Thus, POLAR prefers resident adapters unless a non-resident adapter offers sufficient estimated quality gain to offset its latency penalty.

At the end of each epoch, POLAR updates the resident set using a greedy marginal-gain rule based on the previous epoch’s contexts and current UCB estimates; the full pseudocode appears in Appendix B. Because this update incurs approximation loss and rarely selected adapters may remain poorly estimated, POLAR does not in general guarantee sublinear regret under our strongest benchmark (see Theorem 4.1).

3.2. POLAR+: Epoch Doubling with Forced Exploration

While POLAR captures the basic two-timescale control logic, its regret can remain linear due to two effects. First, the greedy cache update introduces a constant-factor approximation loss at every epoch. Second, adapters that are rarely selected by the router may never accumulate sufficiently accurate estimates, which in turn prevents the cache controller from confidently identifying the best resident set. To address both issues, we introduce POLAR+ (Algorithm 2), which is the main algorithmic variant studied in this paper. POLAR+ strengthens POLAR in three ways.

(i) Epoch doubling. Epoch ℓ\ell contains 2ℓ2^{\ell} exploitation rounds. As the epoch index grows, parameter estimates become more accurate, while the number of cache updates grows only logarithmically in TT. This reduces control-plane churn and is key to making the cumulative cache-identification error summable.

(ii) Forced exploration. At the start of each epoch, POLAR+ executes a short forced exploration phase consisting of N​mℓNm_{\ell} round-robin plays, where each adapter is sampled mℓm_{\ell} times independent of the current router estimates. This ensures every adapter receives informative observations, including adapters that would otherwise remain under-sampled because their current estimates or cold penalties make them unattractive. Operationally, this phase can be interpreted as a probing window inserted between cache updates.

(iii) Improved cache optimization. After the forced exploration phase, the cache controller selects the next resident set by maximizing an empirical cache utility F^n​(S)\hat{F}_{n}(S) over all size-KK sets. For the theory, we write this step abstractly as SolveCache​(F^n,K)\textsc{SolveCache}(\hat{F}_{n},K). Formally,

F^n​(S)\displaystyle\hat{F}_{n}(S) :=1n​∑t=1nmaxa∈ℳ⁡μ^​(a,S,xt),\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}\max_{a\in\mathcal{M}}\hat{\mu}(a;S;x_{t}),
(9) μ^​(a,S,x)\displaystyle\hat{\mu}(a;S;x) :=⟨θ^a,x⟩−αλa𝟏{a∉S},\displaystyle:=\langle\hat{\theta}_{a},x\rangle-\alpha\lambda_{a}\mathbf{1}\{a\notin S\},

is the empirical cache utility evaluated using the current parameter estimates over all historical contexts; nℓ:=∑j<ℓ(N​mj+2j)n_{\ell}:=\sum_{j<\ell}(Nm_{j}+2^{j}) denotes the number of rounds completed before epoch ℓ\ell. In the analysis of POLAR+, we instantiate SolveCache as the exact optimizer arg⁡max|S|=K​F^n​(S)\arg\max_{|S|=K}\hat{F}_{n}(S) in order to isolate the statistical difficulty of cache identification from approximation effects. In practice, this step can be implemented by the same greedy procedure as Algorithm 3 or by any standard fast solver for monotone submodular maximization. When the adapter library is moderate, exact optimization is also feasible at epoch boundaries. Under i.i.d. contexts and the structural cacheability conditions in Assumptions 1–2, POLAR+ achieves 𝒪~​(T)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T}) sublinear regret; see Theorem 4.2.

Finally, note that neither POLAR nor POLAR+ needs to know the latent hot set ℳhot\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{hot}} from Assumption 2. Both routing and caching are carried out over the full adapter library ℳ\mathcal{M}. Moreover, POLAR+ is anytime: all quantities are computed online from the current epoch index and past observations, without requiring prior knowledge of the horizon TT.

4. Regret Analysis

We now analyze the two algorithmic variants introduced in Section 3. This section establishes regret guarantees for the joint caching-and-routing problem and highlights the technical mechanisms that make these guarantees possible. In particular, we explain why the problem is not a routine combination of contextual bandits and online caching, and how the two-timescale structure shapes both the upper bounds and their proof techniques.

At a high level, the main difficulty comes from the two-timescale coupling. The fast router must learn context-dependent adapter quality from bandit feedback, while the slow cache controller determines which adapters are cheap to access. This creates an endogenous feedback loop: the resident set changes the cost of exploration, and the routing policy determines which adapters receive informative observations. Consequently, caching is not merely a combinatorial action layered on top of a contextual bandit; it alters the data-collection process that drives learning.

We first analyze POLAR under arbitrary contexts and show that it achieves a worst-case regret guarantee, but with a linear cache gap. We then show that this linear term is not a proof artifact of the analysis of POLAR. Rather, it reflects the intrinsic difficulty of cache identification without additional workload structure. Next, we study POLAR+ under stationary workload regularity and cacheability assumptions, and show that under this added structure the cache-identification cost becomes summable, yielding an overall sublinear regret bound.

Throughout the analysis, we use the following notation. Let Va,t:=λId+∑s<t𝟏{as=a}xsxs⊤V_{a,t}:=\lambda I_{d}+\sum_{s<t}\mathbf{1}\{a_{s}=a\}x_{s}x_{s}^{\top} be the regularized design matrix of adapter aa up to round tt, and θ^a,t:=Va,t−1∑s<t𝟏{as=a}qs(a)xs\hat{\theta}_{a,t}:=V_{a,t}^{-1}\sum_{s<t}\mathbf{1}\{a_{s}=a\}q_{s}(a)x_{s} its ridge estimate. Let sa,t:=xt⊤​Va,t−1​xts_{a,t}:=\sqrt{x_{t}^{\top}V_{a,t}^{-1}x_{t}} denote the corresponding prediction width. We write B¯:=2+α​λmax,λmax:=maxa∈ℳ⁡λa,\bar{B}:=2+\alpha\lambda_{\max},\lambda_{\max}:=\max_{a\in\mathcal{M}}\lambda_{a}, so that B¯\bar{B} is a uniform upper bound on the per-round pseudo-regret, since the quality difference is at most 22 and the largest cold-path penalty is α​λmax\alpha\lambda_{\max}.

4.1. Worst-Case Guarantee for POLAR

We begin with the fixed-epoch baseline POLAR. This result applies under the basic linear contextual model with no distributional assumptions on the context sequence. It should therefore be viewed as a robustness baseline: even under arbitrary request sequences, POLAR controls the routing error and cache switching overhead. At the same time, Theorem 4.1 makes clear that without additional workload structure, the cache-identification cost can remain linear.

Theorem 4.1 (Worst-case regret of POLAR).

Assume the linear model (1), with ‖θa⋆‖2≤1\|\theta_{a}^{\star}\|_{2}\leq 1, ‖xt‖2≤1\|x_{t}\|_{2}\leq 1, conditionally σ\sigma-sub-Gaussian noise, ridge parameter λ≥1\lambda\geq 1, and bounded cold-path penalties λa∈(0,λmax]\lambda_{a}\in(0,\lambda_{\max}]. Then, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, Algorithm 1 satisfies

(10) Regret⁡(T)≤2​βT​2​N​d​T​log⁡(1+Td​λ)⏟routing+α​λmax​T⏟cache gap+⌈TH⌉​K​γ⏟switching.\displaystyle\mathrm{Regret}(T)\leq\underbrace{2\beta_{T}\sqrt{2NdT\log\Bigl(1+\frac{T}{d\lambda}\Bigr)}}_{\text{routing}}+\underbrace{\alpha\lambda_{\max}T}_{\text{cache gap}}+\underbrace{\Bigl\lceil\frac{T}{H}\Bigr\rceil K\gamma}_{\text{switching}}.

Implications. Theorem 4.1 separates the overall regret into three distinct components.

⊳\triangleright Routing regret: The first term is the standard statistical price of learning context-dependent adapter quality under bandit feedback. Up to constants and logarithmic factors, this is the familiar LinUCB term.

⊳\triangleright Cache gap: The second term measures the cost of operating with a possibly suboptimal resident set. This is the extra difficulty introduced by the memory hierarchy: even if the router were optimal for the current cache, the cache itself may still be wrong.

⊳\triangleright Switching overhead: The third term is the control-plane cost of reconfiguring the resident set at epoch boundaries. This term has no analog in ordinary contextual bandits which do not model slow-timescale resident-set updates.

Taken together, Theorem 4.1 shows that regret in edge adapter serving has three sources: a data-plane learning term, a cache-identification term induced by the memory hierarchy, and a control-plane switching term caused by cache reconfiguration.

Remark 1 (Why standard analyses do not apply directly).

Classical contextual bandit analyses control routing regret for a fixed action set, but do not model a slow-timescale resident-set decision that changes the effective access cost of each arm; see, e.g., standard analyses of linear contextual bandits and LinUCB (Chu et al., 2011; Abbasi-Yadkori et al., 2011). Conversely, online caching and paging analyses typically assume that item values are known or exogenous, rather than learned from policy-dependent feedback. Our setting lies between these two worlds: the cache changes the future cost of observing adapters, and the router determines which adapters generate informative samples for future cache updates. This feedback coupling is precisely what makes the analysis nonstandard.

Remark 2 (Why the linear cache term is intrinsic under arbitrary contexts).

The linear cache term in Theorem 4.1 should not be interpreted as a weakness of POLAR alone. Rather, it reflects a genuine limitation of the unrestricted setting. Under arbitrary contexts, the long-run value of caching an adapter cannot, in general, be inferred from online observations alone, because the observations are themselves shaped by the current cache and routing policy. Without additional structure, the learner may never receive enough representative information to distinguish a globally valuable adapter from one that only appears useful under the current, possibly misleading, resident set. In this sense, the linear cache term captures the intrinsic difficulty of cache identification without workload regularity.

Practical guidance. Theorem 4.1 also yields a simple systems-level tradeoff. A smaller epoch length HH, equivalently a more frequent cache-update interval, allows the controller to react more quickly to newly learned information, but increases the switching term. A larger HH reduces reconfiguration overhead, but leaves the system with a stale resident set for longer. Moreover, when the cold-path penalties λa\lambda_{a} are large, the cost of an incorrect resident set can dominate the routing regret, making cache identification the primary systems challenge. Thus, even the worst-case bound highlights why cache control and routing must be analyzed jointly rather than as separate components.

Proof sketch. The proof decomposes regret by adding and subtracting maxa⁡μt​(a,Cℓ⁡(t))\max_{a}\mu_{t}(a;C_{\ell(t)}), which yields three terms corresponding to routing, cache mismatch, and switching. The routing term is handled by standard confidence and elliptic-potential arguments for LinUCB. The key simplification in the worst-case analysis is that the cache term is controlled by a uniform per-round bound: the gap between any two resident sets is at most α​λmax\alpha\lambda_{\max}, so one need not estimate long-run cache utility under arbitrary contexts. The switching term simply counts epoch boundaries and charges at most K​γK\gamma per update. The full proof, together with the supporting confidence and submodularity lemmas, appears in Appendix C.

4.2. Sublinear Regret via Epoch Doubling and Cacheability (POLAR+)

Theorem 4.1 shows that worst-case robustness alone is not enough to eliminate the linear cache gap. We now show that this gap disappears once the workload has stable statistical structure and the adapter library contains a meaningful cacheable subset. This is the regime most relevant to stationary edge services: request types recur over time, some adapters repeatedly serve distinct traffic segments well, and cold-path access is expensive enough that keeping the right adapters resident matters.

Theorem 4.2 shows that under this additional structure, POLAR+ learns both which adapter to route to and which adapters deserve residency at sublinear cost. For analytical convenience we set κ=1\kappa=1 throughout this section.

Theorem 4.2 (Sublinear regret of POLAR+).

Under Assumptions 1 and 2, and the conditions of Theorem 4.1, Algorithm 2 satisfies, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

(11) Regret⁡(T)=𝒪~​(σ​d​N​T⏟routing+B¯​K​T⏟cache identification).\displaystyle\mathrm{Regret}(T)=\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\bigg(\underbrace{\sigma d\sqrt{NT}}_{\text{routing}}+\underbrace{\bar{B}\sqrt{KT}}_{\text{cache identification}}\bigg).

Implications. The routing term σ​d​N​T\sigma d\sqrt{NT} matches the minimax lower bound Ω⁡(d​N​T)\Omega(d\sqrt{NT}) for NN-arm linear contextual bandits up to logarithmic factors and the noise level σ\sigma. This shows that the memory hierarchy does not fundamentally degrade routing efficiency: POLAR+ learns adapter quality at the same rate as standard LinUCB, despite the additional caching layer. The cache-identification term B¯​K​T\bar{B}\sqrt{KT} is the extra price of learning which KK adapters deserve fast-memory residency. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first sublinear cache-identification guarantee for joint adapter caching and routing with unknown contextual utility.

Regime interpretation. Theorem 4.2 is especially informative across different operating regimes. When K≪NK\ll N but the cold-path penalties are moderate, the routing term may dominate, and the main challenge is learning adapter quality. When cold-path access is expensive, the cache-identification term is the bottleneck, and learning the hot set is as important as learning per-request routing. In the degenerate case K=NK=N, all adapters fit in memory and the cache term vanishes, reducing the problem to ordinary contextual routing. This matches the system intuition: when residency is no longer a constraint, the learning problem collapses to routing alone.

What changes relative to Theorem 4.1. Compared with Theorem 4.1, the linear cache gap becomes 𝒪~​(T)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T}), and the switching overhead drops from 𝒪⁡(T/H)\mathcal{O}(T/H) to 𝒪⁡(log⁡T)\mathcal{O}(\log T) under epoch doubling. This improvement requires additional workload regularity and cacheability structure. Moreover, POLAR+ is anytime and does not require prior knowledge of the horizon.

Assumptions and operational meaning. The sublinear result relies on two structural conditions that have clear interpretations in edge LLM serving. The first concerns workload stability. The second concerns whether the adapter library contains a meaningful hot set that is worth keeping resident.

Assumption 1 (i.i.d. regularity).

The contexts satisfy xt∼i.i.d.𝒟x_{t}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}\mathcal{D} with

(12) 𝔼⁡[xt​xt⊤]⪰σmin​Id\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[x_{t}x_{t}^{\top}]\succeq\sigma_{\min}I_{d}

for some σmin>0\sigma_{\min}>0.

Assumption 1 formalizes a stationary workload over the cache-control timescale: the service repeatedly sees a stable mixture of request types, and the feature map contains enough variation to identify adapter quality. This assumption should be interpreted over the timescale of cache learning and reconfiguration, not as a claim that edge traffic is globally static over arbitrarily long horizons. Rather, it states that over the horizon on which the cache is being learned, the workload is stable enough to admit a meaningful steady-state resident set.

Assumption 2 (Cacheable diversity).

There exists a subset ℳhot⊆ℳ\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{hot}}\subseteq\mathcal{M} with |ℳhot|≥K|\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{hot}}|\geq K such that for each a∈ℳhota\in\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{hot}}, the region

(13) Xa:={x:a=argmaxa′∈ℳμ(a′;C;x) for all C⊆ℳhot,|C|=K}\displaystyle X_{a}\!:=\!\left\{x\!:\!a\!=\!\arg\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{M}}\mu(a^{\prime};C;x)\text{ for all }C\subseteq\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{hot}},\ |C|=K\right\}

satisfies:

  1. (i)

    Coverage: Prx∼𝒟⁡(x∈Xa)≥pmin\Pr_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}(x\in X_{a})\geq p_{\min}.

  2. (ii)

    Margin: for every C⊆ℳhotC\subseteq\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{hot}} with |C|=K|C|=K,

    (14) infx∈Xa[μ⁡(a,C,x)−maxa′≠a⁡μ⁡(a′,C,x)]≥Δmin>0.\displaystyle\inf_{x\in X_{a}}\left[\mu(a;C;x)-\max_{a^{\prime}\neq a}\mu(a^{\prime};C;x)\right]\geq\Delta_{\min}>0.
  3. (iii)

    Full-dimensionality: 𝔼⁡[x​x⊤∣x∈Xa]⪰σmin​Id\mathbb{E}[xx^{\top}\mid x\in X_{a}]\succeq\sigma_{\min}I_{d}.

  4. (iv)

    Cache separability:

    (15) F⁡(C†)−max|S|≤KS⊈ℳhot⁡F⁡(S)≥Δcache>0.\displaystyle F(C^{\dagger})-\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}|S|\leq K\\ S\not\subseteq\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{hot}}\end{subarray}}F(S)\geq\Delta_{\mathrm{cache}}>0.
  5. (v)

    Hot dominance:

    (16) α⋅mina∉ℳhot⁡λa>2,\displaystyle\alpha\cdot\min_{a\notin\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{hot}}}\lambda_{a}>2,

    and we write

    (17) Δdom:=α​mina∉ℳhot​λa−2>0.\displaystyle\Delta_{\mathrm{dom}}:=\alpha\min_{a\notin\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{hot}}}\lambda_{a}-2>0.

Assumption 2 captures the practical notion of a cacheable hot set. In many edge services, traffic is skewed: a subset of adapters repeatedly serves recurring request segments, and those adapters are precisely the ones that should remain resident. The coverage and margin conditions say that each hot adapter is useful on a nontrivial part of the workload and is clearly better there. The cache-separability condition says that the optimal resident set is meaningfully better than any cache that includes non-hot adapters. Finally, the hot-dominance condition says that for non-hot adapters, the cold-path latency is large enough that any quality gain they might offer is not sufficient to offset the paging penalty. Operationally, this means the service has a meaningful steady-state working set and that cold execution is expensive enough to make residency matter. These assumptions should therefore be viewed not merely as technical devices, but as identifiability conditions for steady-state cache learning in a stationary edge service.

Remark 3 (Why Assumption 2 is not overly restrictive).

Assumption 2 requires diversity only for the cacheable hot subset, not for the entire adapter library. After the bootstrap phase, the algorithm’s cache is shown to lie inside ℳhot\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{hot}}, so competition effectively occurs only among hot adapters. In particular, hot dominance ensures that cold adapters are never competitive under any hot cache once the estimation error is sufficiently small. This is the analog, in our two-timescale setting, of a margin condition in standard contextual bandits: it guarantees that the steady-state resident set is identifiable from online observations rather than requiring all adapters in the library to be equally learnable or equally relevant.

Practical guidance. Theorem 4.2 suggests three design principles for edge LLM serving: cache updates should become less frequent as confidence improves; explicit probing is most valuable early, when the hot set is still being identified; and larger cold-path penalties increase the value of accurate cache selection. If memory is abundant enough to hold all adapters, the problem reduces to ordinary contextual routing.

4.2.1. Proof Structure and Technical Insights

A more detailed decomposition. The proof yields the following refined expansion:

Regret⁡(T)≤2​βT​2​N​d​T​log⁡(1+Td​λ)⏟routing+c2​σ​d​log⁡(N​L​T/δ)+λσmin​pmin​T⏟cache estimation\displaystyle\mathrm{Regret}(T)\!\leq\!\underbrace{2\beta_{T}\sqrt{2NdT\log\Bigl(1+\frac{T}{d\lambda}\Bigr)}}_{\text{routing}}+\underbrace{c_{2}\frac{\sigma\sqrt{d\log(NLT/\delta)}+\sqrt{\lambda}}{\sqrt{\sigma_{\min}p_{\min}}}\sqrt{T}}_{\text{cache estimation}}
(18) +c3​B¯​K​T​log⁡(e​N​LK​δ)⏟cache concentration+K​γ​L⏟switching+∑ℓN​mℓ​B¯⏟forced exploration+2ℓ⋆​B¯⏟bootstrap,\displaystyle+\underbrace{c_{3}\bar{B}\sqrt{KT\log\Bigl(\frac{eNL}{K\delta}\Bigr)}}_{\text{cache concentration}}+\underbrace{K\gamma L}_{\text{switching}}\!+\!\underbrace{\sum_{\ell}Nm_{\ell}\bar{B}}_{\text{forced exploration}}\!+\!\underbrace{2^{\ell_{\star}}\bar{B}}_{\text{bootstrap}},

where L=⌈log2⁡T⌉L=\lceil\log_{2}T\rceil and ℓ⋆\ell_{\star} is the bootstrap epoch defined later in the proof.

Each term has a distinct role. The first is the usual routing regret. The second is the price of estimating adapter utilities accurately enough for cache selection. The third is a uniform concentration term over all size-KK resident sets. The fourth is the total control-plane churn from epoch updates. The fifth is the explicit probing cost incurred by forced exploration. The sixth is a transient bootstrap term until the algorithm has collected enough information to identify the relevant hot set. The key point is that the first three terms are 𝒪~​(T)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T}), while the last three are lower-order for fixed problem parameters.

Remark 4 (Why standard proof techniques still do not apply).

Even under Assumptions 1 and 2, the analysis is not a routine combination of contextual-bandit and caching arguments. The reason is that the resident set changes the information geometry of the problem. A non-resident adapter is not only more expensive to use; it is also less likely to be sampled by the optimistic router. Thus the algorithm may fail to learn about an adapter precisely because it is not resident, and may fail to cache it because it has not yet learned its value. This circular dependence does not appear in standard contextual bandits, nor in online caching with exogenous values.

Proof idea and technical novelties. The proof has three conceptual stages.

⊳\triangleright Stage 1: Bootstrap. Forced exploration guarantees that every adapter receives i.i.d. samples regardless of the current cache. After a finite bootstrap epoch ℓ⋆\ell_{\star}, two conditions hold simultaneously: (i) the routing confidence width is small enough to identify the best adapter on the relevant regions of the context space, and (ii) the empirical cache utility is accurate enough to distinguish hot caches from non-hot ones. This breaks the initial adverse feedback loop between cache and routing.

⊳\triangleright Stage 2: Geometric convergence. Once the bootstrap conditions hold, a virtuous cycle emerges. Better estimates improve routing and better routing yields more informative exploitation samples on hot regions. These samples sharpen the empirical cache utility, and better cache choices reduce cold-path penalties. Under epoch doubling, epoch ℓ\ell has 2ℓ2^{\ell} exploitation rounds while the residual per-epoch cache error decays as 𝒪(2−ℓ/2)\mathcal{O}(2^{-\ell/2}). This is the key mechanism that turns a persistent cache gap into a summable one.

⊳\triangleright Stage 3: Collecting terms. The final regret bound follows by summing the routing term from the elliptic potential argument, the cache-estimation and concentration terms from the empirical cache utility, and the lower-order switching, probing, and bootstrap costs. The complete derivation appears in Appendix D.

5. Experiments

We evaluate POLAR and POLAR+ in a measurement-calibrated simulation using real LoRA adapters, measured GPU paging latencies, and benchmark-derived adapter utilities. The experiments are designed to validate three aspects of the theory: (i) the sublinear scaling of POLAR+, (ii) the role of epoch doubling, forced exploration, and improved cache optimization, and (iii) the ability of POLAR+ to learn a high-quality resident set while keeping control-plane churn low.

5.1. Experimental Setup

Adapters and base model. We use 15 community-contributed LoRA adapters for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Yang et al., 2024), downloaded from HuggingFace and spanning 15 domains, including math, reasoning, medical, clinical NER, finance, legal, education, cybersecurity, and creative writing. Together with the base model, this gives N=16N=16 arms. We include the base model as a special arm with λbase=0\lambda_{\text{base}}=0, reflecting that it is always resident as part of the serving stack and therefore incurs no cold-path penalty; the cache controller thus effectively allocates its KK slots among the 1515 LoRA adapters. Adapters exhibit substantial heterogeneity in LoRA rank (8 to 64) and size (50 to 656 MB), which makes them suitable for studying memory-residency decisions under realistic edge constraints.

Latency and quality calibration. For each adapter aa, we measure the cold-path latency λa\lambda_{a} on an NVIDIA RTX 5080 GPU by loading the adapter through PEFT 20 times and recording the loading delay. The measured GPU load latencies range from 291 ms (rank-32, 50 MB) to 1263 ms (rank-64, 656 MB), confirming substantial heterogeneity in paging cost across adapters. In the simulation, λa\lambda_{a} is expressed in seconds (λa=raw ms/103\lambda_{a}=\text{raw ms}/10^{3}), matching the reward scale of the quality parameters θa⋆\theta_{a}^{\star} (normalized so that ‖θa⋆‖2≤1\|\theta_{a}^{\star}\|_{2}\leq 1). To instantiate the quality model, each adapter is evaluated on five benchmarks (MMLU, ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, TruthfulQA, and GSM8K) using log-probability scoring, yielding the adapter-specific utility parameters θa⋆\theta_{a}^{\star} used in the simulation. In particular, the measured adapter utilities differ meaningfully across domains: for example, the job-classifier adapter reduces MMLU accuracy from 0.70 to 0.42, while the cybersecurity adapter improves it to 0.74.

Request generation and simulation. Contexts follow a power-law task distribution as in EdgeLoRA (Shen et al., 2025). Thus, the evaluation should be understood as measurement-calibrated rather than a literal trace replay: real adapter latencies and benchmark-derived utilities are combined with a synthetic but workload-informed request stream. Each request is associated with a context vector encoding task information, and rewards are generated according to the linear contextual model in Section 2. This design allows us to study the online control problem under realistic paging costs while keeping the underlying utility model transparent and reproducible.

Simulation parameters. Unless otherwise stated, we use cache size K=5K=5, context dimension d=5d=5, epoch length H=200H=200, noise level σ=0.05\sigma=0.05, switching cost γ=0.3\gamma=0.3, and ridge parameter λ=1\lambda=1. We set α=0.5\alpha=0.5 so that the average cache-miss penalty is comparable to the average utility gap (penalty/quality ratio ≈1.1\approx 1.1). For POLAR+, forced exploration uses κ=0.05\kappa=0.05, corresponding to N​mℓ≈32Nm_{\ell}\approx 32 rounds per epoch, about 2%2\% of the horizon. All reported results are means ±\pm standard deviations over 5 random seeds.

Baselines. We compare against four online baselines that pair LinUCB routing with standard cache policies: ε\varepsilon-Greedy Cache (ε=0.1\varepsilon=0.1 with greedy submodular cache updates), LFU Cache, LRU Cache, and Static Cache (a random fixed cache with no updates). We additionally include an Oracle Cache + LinUCB reference, in which the cache is fixed at the hindsight-optimal set CT⋆C_{T}^{\star} (defined in Section 2) and LinUCB learns only the routing policy. This reference isolates the routing-side difficulty that remains even when cache learning is removed, and therefore serves as a routing-only lower reference for any online method that must learn the cache as well.

5.2. Main Results

Figure 3 reports cumulative regret up to T=105T=10^{5}. Both POLAR and POLAR+ significantly outperform the heuristic baselines, with POLAR+ achieving the lowest regret among all online methods. Relative to the Oracle Cache reference, POLAR+ incurs only a modest overhead for learning the resident set online, while substantially closing the gap between heuristic caching and the offline-optimal cache. At T=105T=10^{5}, POLAR+ reaches 288±33288\pm 33, compared with 493±198493\pm 198 for POLAR, 1,5381{,}538 for the best heuristic baseline, and 66±5066\pm 50 for Oracle Cache. Its regret curve visibly flattens after T≈3×104T\approx 3\times 10^{4}, consistent with sublinear growth.

Figure 3 shows regret as a function of TT on a log-log scale. POLAR+ grows much more slowly than POLAR and the heuristic baselines, and its slope tracks Oracle Cache much more closely. In particular, POLAR+ grows from 219219 to 530530 over a 16.7×16.7\times increase in the horizon, while POLAR and the heuristic baselines grow substantially faster. POLAR+ overtakes POLAR near T=5×104T=5\times 10^{4}, and the gap widens as the horizon grows. This behavior empirically supports the 𝒪~​(T)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T}) scaling predicted by Theorem 4.2.

5.3. Theory-Facing Validation

Sensitivity to latency weight α\alpha. Figure 5 varies α\alpha for T=105T=10^{5} with α∈{0.1,0.2,0.5,1.0}\alpha\in\{0.1,0.2,0.5,1.0\}. POLAR’s regret stabilizes once α≥0.5\alpha\geq 0.5: after the cache identifies valuable adapters, routing naturally avoids cold penalties. In contrast, POLAR+’s regret increases with α\alpha, consistent with the B¯=2+α​λmax\bar{B}=2+\alpha\lambda_{\max} dependence in Theorem 4.2. Static Cache is largely insensitive to α\alpha because its random cache quality does not depend on the latency weight.

Operational regret decomposition. To connect the experiments to Theorem 4.2, Figure 5 decomposes cumulative regret into a quality loss and a latency cost. This is an operational decomposition rather than a literal term-by-term restatement of the theorem: quality loss reflects routing error, while latency cost captures the combined effect of cache misses and forced exploration. For POLAR+, the quality-loss component stays nearly constant at ≈134\approx 134 across all α\alpha, confirming that the routing term σ​d​N​T\sigma d\sqrt{NT} is independent of α\alpha. Its latency cost grows approximately linearly (34→30034\to 300), matching the predicted B¯∝α\bar{B}\propto\alpha scaling. By contrast, POLAR’s latency cost is near zero because its cache-aware UCB routing naturally avoids uncached adapters, but its quality loss is 3.6×3.6\times higher (486486 vs. 134134) due to insufficient exploration. This explains why POLAR+ overtakes POLAR at larger α\alpha: the cost of forced exploration grows, but the resulting improvement in utility estimation and cache selection more than compensates.

Effect of cache-update cadence. Figure 10 studies the fixed epoch length H∈{50,100,200,500,1000}H\in\{50,100,200,500,1000\} at T=105T=10^{5}. POLAR+ is shown as a flat reference because it does not use a fixed epoch size; instead, its update schedule is determined by epoch doubling. The w/o doubling variant should be read as “POLAR+ with fixed epochs,” i.e., it retains forced exploration and exact cache optimization but replaces geometric epoch growth with a fixed update interval HH. Both POLAR and this w/o doubling variant improve as HH grows over the tested range: POLAR drops from 687687 at H=50H=50 to 323323 at H=1000H=1000, and w/o doubling drops from 11,72511{,}725 to 1,2251{,}225. Small HH triggers more frequent greedy-cache updates (for POLAR) and more frequent forced-exploration phases (for w/o doubling), both of which add cumulative cost. Even at the best tested H=1000H=1000, POLAR still lags POLAR+ (323323 vs. 288288) and w/o doubling remains 4×4\times worse (1,2251{,}225), showing that no fixed choice of HH recovers the self-tuning behavior of POLAR+. This provides an empirical counterpart to the switching and cache-identification improvements highlighted by Theorem 4.2.

Ablation of POLAR+ components. Theorem 4.2 attributes POLAR+’s sublinear regret to three ingredients: epoch doubling, exact cache optimization, and forced exploration. We verify that each is necessary by leave-one-out ablations at T=105T=10^{5}. Removing one component at a time yields three variants. POLAR (fixed epoch + greedy cache + no forced exploration) serves as a lower reference. Figure 10 reports the final regret at T=105T=10^{5} for each variant. POLAR+ achieves regret 288288; removing exact cache degrades it to 402402, indicating a moderate loss from replacing exact cache optimization with greedy updates. In contrast, removing epoch doubling inflates regret to 4,6744{,}674 (16×16\times worse), while removing forced exploration yields 1,7881{,}788 (6×6\times worse). These two ingredients are therefore especially load-bearing in practice. POLAR reaches 493493: higher than POLAR+ but lower than either broken variant, because it pays no forced-exploration cost on top of a misconfigured schedule.

Control-plane churn. Figure 10 reports the cumulative number of cache updates over time. POLAR+ performs only ≈9\approx 9 updates across 10510^{5} rounds, consistent with the 𝒪⁡(log⁡T)\mathcal{O}(\log T) cache-refresh schedule induced by epoch doubling. Exact cache is inherently stable: the w/o doubling variant also performs only ≈10\approx 10 updates, showing that its large regret comes mainly from repeated forced-exploration rounds rather than from additional switching. In contrast, greedy cache is noticeably more churny: w/o exact performs ≈15\approx 15 updates under doubling, and POLAR (fixed-epoch greedy) reaches ≈22\approx 22 updates, consistent with its 𝒪⁡(T/H)\mathcal{O}(T/H)-style control-plane refresh. The w/o forced variant switches only twice: without unbiased context samples, exact cache locks onto a biased but stable suboptimum early and never revises. This explains its persistent regret despite its low switching count. Together, Figures 10 and 10 confirm that all three ingredients are load-bearing and epoch doubling is essential not only for regret scaling but for reducing control-plane churn.

Learning the resident set. Theorem 4.2 predicts that POLAR+ should learn a near-optimal resident set, not merely a good routing rule. Figure 11 tests this claim directly using two diagnostics: (i) the Jaccard similarity between the current cache Cℓ⁡(t)C_{\ell(t)} and the hindsight-optimal cache CT⋆C_{T}^{\star}, and (ii) the quality loss incurred by using Cℓ⁡(t)C_{\ell(t)} as a fixed cache on the next 2,0002{,}000 contexts. The right panel is the more direct validation of the theorem’s cache-identification objective, because Jaccard overlap is a strict set-level metric and can remain below one even when two caches induce very similar utility. Under this more operational measure, POLAR+ converges rapidly to a high-quality resident set: its quality loss drops to ≈2.6\approx 2.6 by t≈103t\approx 10^{3}, a 6×6\times reduction from the initial value at t=200t=200. POLAR eventually reaches a comparable Jaccard overlap, but only near t≈3×104t\approx 3\times 10^{4}, and its steady-state quality loss remains around 5.75.7, roughly twice that of POLAR+. LRU and LFU, which react to request frequency rather than utility, stay near-constant at low Jaccard overlap and high quality loss throughout. Thus, while Jaccard is informative, the cache-quality-loss panel more directly shows that POLAR+ identifies a near-optimal resident set much earlier than the alternatives.

5.4. Additional Sensitivity and Ablation

Cache size KK. Figure 10 varies cache size KK at T=105T=10^{5}. All methods benefit from larger caches, but POLAR+ benefits the most: its regret improves from 522522 at K=2K=2 to 266266 at K=7K=7 because a larger cache reduces the cost of maintaining the hot set. POLAR is less sensitive to KK, as its UCB routing naturally avoids uncached adapters.

Routing strategy. We replace LinUCB with Linear Thompson Sampling (Agrawal and Goyal, 2013) in both POLAR and POLAR+. Figure 10 shows that the two routing strategies perform similarly within fixed-epoch POLAR, but POLAR+ benefits more clearly from UCB. We attribute this to the more stable interaction between deterministic optimism, forced exploration, and cache identification. We view this as a router ablation rather than a central validation of the theory.

6. Related Work

LoRA adapter serving. Recent systems work studies efficient multi-adapter LLM serving through cross-adapter batching and shared base-model execution (Chen et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024), unified memory management and paging for adapter weights and KV caches (Sheng et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025), cold-start reduction and proactive prefetching (Sui et al., 2025; Ni et al., 2025), and edge- or hardware-aware designs for fast adapter switching (Shen et al., 2025; Tian et al., 2025). These works optimize the systems layer of multi-adapter serving, focusing on memory management, scheduling, and hardware efficiency. Our work operates at a different layer: given a mechanism for loading and evicting adapters, we study the online decision problem of which adapters to keep resident under uncertain, query-dependent utility.

Contextual bandits and online routing for LLMs. Recent work applies bandit methods to online LLM or backend selection (Poon et al., 2026; Wei et al., 2025; Li, 2025; Zhang et al., 2026). Closest in spirit on the learning side, Li and Li (Li and Li, 2026) study a two-timescale online deployment-and-routing problem for a streaming LLM inventory under per-query budget constraints, obtaining near-optimal 𝒪~​(T2/3)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{2/3}) regret. Their setting, however, is fundamentally different from ours: they consider deployment over multiple models in a non-contextual environment, whereas we study a fixed base model with a library of adapters whose context-dependent utility must be learned under a memory hierarchy with hot/cold access asymmetry, a coupling not captured by existing regret analyses. Related work also considers semantic caching and cache-assisted routing (Zhu et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2026), but these works typically cache responses or route among equally available backends. In contrast, POLAR studies a coupled problem in which request-level routing and size-KK adapter residency must be jointly optimized under memory constraints and paging-induced latency.

Online caching. Classical online paging and caching focus on competitive analysis under adversarial request sequences (Sleator and Tarjan, 1985; Borodin and El-Yaniv, 2005), while more recent work studies learning-augmented or regret-minimizing caching policies under stochastic demand (Paschos et al., 2020; Quan et al., 2024; Chu et al., 2024). Xu et al. (Xu et al., 2026) use deep reinforcement learning for mobile-edge LLM caching and inference offloading. These methods target content objects, responses, or full models with known or externally specified value. They do not model the setting studied here, where adapter utility is both context-dependent and unknown, and where caching and routing are statistically coupled because the cache changes which adapters are cheap to explore and the router changes which adapters are observed.

7. Conclusion

We introduced POLAR, a two-timescale online learning framework for joint adapter routing and cache placement in edge LLM serving. POLAR combines a cache-aware router with an epoch-based cache controller, and admits both worst-case and sublinear regret guarantees under different operating regimes. Our analysis shows that memory-residency constraints can be handled without fundamentally slowing routing learning. Experiments with real LoRA adapters and measured paging latencies support the theory and show clear improvements over non-adaptive baselines.

Appendix C Proof of Theorem 4.1 (POLAR)

We first state the supporting lemmas, then give the proof.

Lemma C.1 (UCB confidence ellipsoid).

Assume ‖θa⋆‖2≤1\|\theta_{a}^{\star}\|_{2}\leq 1, ‖xt‖2≤1\|x_{t}\|_{2}\leq 1, and ηt​(a)\eta_{t}(a) is conditionally σ\sigma-sub-Gaussian. Then with probability ≥1−δ\geq 1-\delta, for all a∈ℳa\in\mathcal{M} and t≤Tt\leq T,

|xt⊤​(θ^a,t−θa⋆)|≤βt​sa,t,|x_{t}^{\top}(\hat{\theta}_{a,t}-\theta_{a}^{\star})|\leq\beta_{t}\,s_{a,t},

where βt:=σ​d​log⁡(1+td​λ)+2​log⁡Nδ+λ\beta_{t}:=\sigma\sqrt{d\log(1+\tfrac{t}{d\lambda})+2\log\tfrac{N}{\delta}}+\sqrt{\lambda}. Moreover, βt≥0\beta_{t}\geq 0 and βt1≤βt2\beta_{t_{1}}\leq\beta_{t_{2}} whenever t1≤t2t_{1}\leq t_{2}.

Proof.

Step 1 (Per-arm bound). Fix arm aa. Let Sa,t:=∑s<t𝟏{as=a}ηs(a)xsS_{a,t}:=\sum_{s<t}\mathbf{1}\{a_{s}=a\}\eta_{s}(a)x_{s}. Apply the self-normalized bound for vector-valued martingales (Abbasi-Yadkori et al., 2011, Theorem 1) with failure probability δ′=δ/N\delta^{\prime}=\delta/N:

‖Sa,t‖Va,t−1≤σ​2​log⁡det(Va,t)1/2det(λI)−1/2δ/N.\|S_{a,t}\|_{V_{a,t}^{-1}}\leq\sigma\sqrt{2\log\frac{\det(V_{a,t})^{1/2}\det(\lambda I)^{-1/2}}{\delta/N}}.

Since Va,t​(θ^a,t−θa⋆)=Sa,t−λ​θa⋆V_{a,t}(\hat{\theta}_{a,t}-\theta_{a}^{\star})=S_{a,t}-\lambda\theta_{a}^{\star}, the triangle inequality gives ‖θ^a,t−θa⋆‖Va,t≤‖Sa,t‖Va,t−1+λ​‖θa⋆‖2≤‖Sa,t‖Va,t−1+λ\|\hat{\theta}_{a,t}-\theta_{a}^{\star}\|_{V_{a,t}}\leq\|S_{a,t}\|_{V_{a,t}^{-1}}+\sqrt{\lambda}\|\theta_{a}^{\star}\|_{2}\leq\|S_{a,t}\|_{V_{a,t}^{-1}}+\sqrt{\lambda}.

Step 2 (Log-det simplification). AM–GM on eigenvalues gives det(Va,t)/det(λ​I)≤(1+t/(d​λ))d\det(V_{a,t})/\det(\lambda I)\leq(1{+}t/(d\lambda))^{d}. Hence the log-det term is at most d2​log⁡(1+t/(d​λ))\tfrac{d}{2}\log(1{+}t/(d\lambda)); substituting yields βt\beta_{t}.

Step 3 (Union bound). Taking a union over NN arms, Pr⁡(∃a:bound fails)≤N⋅δ/N=δ\Pr(\exists a:\text{bound fails})\leq N\cdot\delta/N=\delta. The self-normalized bound (Abbasi-Yadkori et al., 2011) holds uniformly over all t≥0t\geq 0, so no additional union bound over time is needed.

Step 4 (Monotonicity). t1≤t2t_{1}\leq t_{2} implies βt1≤βt2\beta_{t_{1}}\leq\beta_{t_{2}} by monotonicity of log\log and ⋅\sqrt{\cdot}.

Step 5 (Consequent). Cauchy–Schwarz in the VV-norm: |x⊤​u|≤‖u‖V​x⊤​V−1​x|x^{\top}u|\leq\|u\|_{V}\sqrt{x^{\top}V^{-1}x}. ∎

Lemma C.2 (Routing regret bound).

On the event of Lemma C.1, with λ≥1\lambda\geq 1,

∑t=1T[maxa⁡μt​(a,Cℓ⁡(t))−μt​(at,Cℓ⁡(t))]≤2​βT​2​N​d​T​log⁡(1+Td​λ).\sum_{t=1}^{T}\bigl[\max_{a}\mu_{t}(a;C_{\ell(t)})-\mu_{t}(a_{t};C_{\ell(t)})\bigr]\leq 2\beta_{T}\sqrt{2NdT\log(1+\tfrac{T}{d\lambda})}.
Proof.

On the confidence event, the LinUCB score ⟨θ^a,xt⟩+βtsa,t−αλa𝟏{a∉Cℓ⁡(t)}\langle\hat{\theta}_{a},x_{t}\rangle+\beta_{t}s_{a,t}-\alpha\lambda_{a}\mathbf{1}\{a\notin C_{\ell(t)}\} upper-bounds μt​(a,Cℓ⁡(t))\mu_{t}(a;C_{\ell(t)}) for all aa. Since ata_{t} maximizes the score, the per-round gap satisfies Δt≤2​βt​sat,t≤2​βT​sat,t\Delta_{t}\leq 2\beta_{t}\,s_{a_{t},t}\leq 2\beta_{T}\,s_{a_{t},t}. By Cauchy–Schwarz, ∑tΔt≤2​βT​T​∑tsat,t2\sum_{t}\Delta_{t}\leq 2\beta_{T}\sqrt{T\sum_{t}s_{a_{t},t}^{2}}. The elliptic potential lemma (Abbasi-Yadkori et al., 2011, Appendix C) gives ∑tsat,t2≤2​N​d​log⁡(1+T/(d​λ))\sum_{t}s_{a_{t},t}^{2}\leq 2Nd\log(1+T/(d\lambda)). ∎

Lemma C.3 (Submodularity of cache benefit).

The cache benefit f⁡(S):=∑t=1H[maxa⁡μt​(a,S)−maxa⁡μt​(a,∅)]f(S):=\sum_{t=1}^{H}[\max_{a}\mu_{t}(a;S)-\max_{a}\mu_{t}(a;\emptyset)] is monotone non-decreasing and submodular.

Proof.

Write μt(a;S)=vt(a)−pen(a)⋅𝟏{a∉S}\mu_{t}(a;S)=v_{t}(a)-\mathrm{pen}(a)\cdot\mathbf{1}\{a\notin S\} where vt​(a):=⟨θa⋆,xt⟩v_{t}(a):=\langle\theta_{a}^{\star},x_{t}\rangle and pen⁡(a):=α​λa≥0\mathrm{pen}(a):=\alpha\lambda_{a}\geq 0.

Pointwise monotonicity. S⊆S′S\subseteq S^{\prime} implies μt​(a,S)≤μt​(a,S′)\mu_{t}(a;S)\leq\mu_{t}(a;S^{\prime}) for all aa, hence maxa⁡μt​(a,S)≤maxa⁡μt​(a,S′)\max_{a}\mu_{t}(a;S)\leq\max_{a}\mu_{t}(a;S^{\prime}).

Single-step submodularity. Fix S⊆S′S\subseteq S^{\prime} and a0a_{0}; let bb and cc be the maximizers of μt​(⋅,S′∪{a0})\mu_{t}(\cdot;S^{\prime}\cup\{a_{0}\}) and μt​(⋅,S)\mu_{t}(\cdot;S), respectively.

Case b=a0b=a_{0}: μt​(b,S′∪{a0})=vt​(a0)≤maxa⁡μt​(a,S∪{a0})\mu_{t}(b;S^{\prime}\cup\{a_{0}\})=v_{t}(a_{0})\leq\max_{a}\mu_{t}(a;S\cup\{a_{0}\}) (since a0∈S∪{a0}a_{0}\in S\cup\{a_{0}\}), and maxa⁡μt​(a,S′)≥μt​(c,S′)≥μt​(c,S)\max_{a}\mu_{t}(a;S^{\prime})\geq\mu_{t}(c;S^{\prime})\geq\mu_{t}(c;S).

Case b≠a0b\neq a_{0}: maxa⁡μt​(a,S′)≥μt​(b,S′)=μt​(b,S′∪{a0})\max_{a}\mu_{t}(a;S^{\prime})\geq\mu_{t}(b;S^{\prime})=\mu_{t}(b;S^{\prime}\cup\{a_{0}\}), and maxa⁡μt​(a,S∪{a0})≥μt​(c,S)\max_{a}\mu_{t}(a;S\cup\{a_{0}\})\geq\mu_{t}(c;S).

Both cases yield

maxa⁡μt​(a,S′∪{a0})+maxa⁡μt​(a,S)\displaystyle\max_{a}\mu_{t}(a;S^{\prime}\!\cup\!\{a_{0}\})+\max_{a}\mu_{t}(a;S)
≤maxa⁡μt​(a,S∪{a0})+maxa⁡μt​(a,S′).\displaystyle\quad\leq\max_{a}\mu_{t}(a;S\!\cup\!\{a_{0}\})+\max_{a}\mu_{t}(a;S^{\prime}).

Summing over tt gives submodularity. ∎

Proof of Theorem 4.1.

Conditioning on the event of Lemma C.1, we write

Regret⁡(T)\displaystyle\mathrm{Regret}(T) =∑t[maxa⁡μt​(a,CT⋆)−μt​(at,Cℓ⁡(t))]\displaystyle=\sum_{t}[\max_{a}\mu_{t}(a;C_{T}^{\star})-\mu_{t}(a_{t};C_{\ell(t)})]
+∑ℓ≥2γ|Cℓ∖Cℓ−1|.\displaystyle\quad+\sum_{\ell\geq 2}\gamma|C_{\ell}\setminus C_{\ell-1}|.

Adding and subtracting maxa⁡μt​(a,Cℓ⁡(t))\max_{a}\mu_{t}(a;C_{\ell(t)}) gives Regret⁡(T)=(I)+(II)+(III)\mathrm{Regret}(T)=\text{(I)}+\text{(II)}+\text{(III)}.

(I) is bounded by Lemma C.2.

(II): By monotonicity (Lemma C.3),

maxa⁡μt​(a,CT⋆)−maxa⁡μt​(a,Cℓ⁡(t))\displaystyle\max_{a}\mu_{t}(a;C_{T}^{\star})-\max_{a}\mu_{t}(a;C_{\ell(t)})
≤maxa⁡μt​(a,CT⋆)−maxa⁡μt​(a,∅)≤α​λmax,\displaystyle\quad\leq\max_{a}\mu_{t}(a;C_{T}^{\star})-\max_{a}\mu_{t}(a;\emptyset)\leq\alpha\lambda_{\max},

since removing all cached arms costs at most α​λmax\alpha\lambda_{\max} per round. Summing gives α​λmax​T\alpha\lambda_{\max}T.

(III): At most ⌈T/H⌉\lceil T/H\rceil epoch boundaries, each costing ≤K​γ\leq K\gamma. ∎

Appendix D Proof of Theorem 4.2 (POLAR+)

Lemma D.1 (Forced exploration controls bonus).

Under 1, after rr cumulative rounds of forced exploration (round-robin) for arm aa, with probability ≥1−δ′\geq 1-\delta^{\prime}: λmin​(Va)≥λ+σmin​r/2\lambda_{\min}(V_{a})\geq\lambda+\sigma_{\min}r/2, and consequently βt​sa,t≤βt/λ+σmin​r/2\beta_{t}\,s_{a,t}\leq\beta_{t}/\sqrt{\lambda+\sigma_{\min}r/2} for all ‖xt‖≤1\|x_{t}\|\leq 1.

Proof.

During forced exploration, arm selection is round-robin (independent of xtx_{t}), so arm aa’s contexts are i.i.d. draws from 𝒟\mathcal{D}. By 1, 𝔼⁡[xt​xt⊤]⪰σmin​Id\mathbb{E}[x_{t}x_{t}^{\top}]\succeq\sigma_{\min}I_{d}. A matrix Chernoff bound (Tropp, 2012, Theorem 5.1.1) gives λmin​(∑s=1rxs​xs⊤)≥σmin​r/2\lambda_{\min}(\sum_{s=1}^{r}x_{s}x_{s}^{\top})\geq\sigma_{\min}r/2 with probability ≥1−δ′\geq 1-\delta^{\prime}, provided r≥c​d​log⁡(d/δ′)r\geq c\,d\log(d/\delta^{\prime}). Since Va⪰λ​I+∑xs​xs⊤V_{a}\succeq\lambda I+\sum x_{s}x_{s}^{\top}, the eigenvalue bound follows. ∎

Lemma D.2 (Bootstrap epoch).

Under 1–2, let Mℓ:=∑j=0ℓmjM_{\ell}:=\sum_{j=0}^{\ell}m_{j} be the cumulative forced plays per arm through epoch ℓ\ell. There exists ℓ0\ell_{0} such that for all ℓ≥ℓ0\ell\geq\ell_{0} and a∈ℳa\in\mathcal{M}, βt​sa,t<Δmin/2\beta_{t}s_{a,t}<\Delta_{\min}/2 on the confidence event.

Proof.

After ℓ+1\ell+1 epochs of forced exploration (round-robin over all NN arms), each arm has ≥Mℓ\geq M_{\ell} cumulative forced plays. By Lemma D.1, the bonus is at most βT/σmin​Mℓ/2\beta_{T}/\sqrt{\sigma_{\min}M_{\ell}/2}. This is <Δmin/2<\Delta_{\min}/2 when Mℓ>8​βT2/(σmin​Δmin2)M_{\ell}>8\beta_{T}^{2}/(\sigma_{\min}\Delta_{\min}^{2}). Since Mℓ=Θ⁡(d​ℓ2)M_{\ell}=\Theta(d\ell^{2}) grows without bound, such ℓ0\ell_{0} exists. After epoch ℓ0\ell_{0}, each subsequent epoch contributes mℓm_{\ell} further forced-exploration samples to every arm, so λmin​(Va)\lambda_{\min}(V_{a}) continues to increase regardless of the exploitation policy (since Va+xt​xt⊤⪰VaV_{a}+x_{t}x_{t}^{\top}\succeq V_{a}). Because βt≤βT\beta_{t}\leq\beta_{T} remains bounded, βt​sa,t≤βT/λmin​(Va)\beta_{t}s_{a,t}\leq\beta_{T}/\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}(V_{a})} can only decrease, and the bonus condition persists for all subsequent epochs. ∎

Lemma D.3 (Correct arm selection).

Under 2, on the confidence event of Lemma C.1, suppose every arm’s exploration bonus satisfies βt​sa,t<Δmin/2\beta_{t}\,s_{a,t}<\Delta_{\min}/2 for all a∈ℳa\in\mathcal{M}. Then for any context x∈Xa⋆x\in X_{a^{\star}} and any hot cache C⊆ℳhotC\subseteq\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{hot}} with |C|=K|C|=K, the LinUCB score of a⋆a^{\star} strictly exceeds that of every other arm (including cold arms).

Proof.

For a′≠a⋆a^{\prime}\neq a^{\star} and x∈Xa⋆x\in X_{a^{\star}}:

score⁡(a⋆)\displaystyle\mathrm{score}(a^{\star}) ≥μ⁡(a⋆,C,x)≥μ⁡(a′,C,x)+Δmin\displaystyle\geq\mu(a^{\star};C;x)\geq\mu(a^{\prime};C;x)+\Delta_{\min}
>μ⁡(a′,C,x)+2​β​sa′≥score⁡(a′).\displaystyle>\mu(a^{\prime};C;x)+2\beta\,s_{a^{\prime}}\geq\mathrm{score}(a^{\prime}).

The first inequality uses confidence (UCB ≥\geq true mean), the second uses the margin on Xa⋆X_{a^{\star}}, the third uses Δmin>2​β​sa′\Delta_{\min}>2\beta\,s_{a^{\prime}}, and the fourth uses confidence (score ≤\leq true mean + 2​β​s+\,2\beta\,s). The margin in 2 quantifies over all a′≠a⋆a^{\prime}\neq a^{\star} (including cold arms), so score dominance holds with unrestricted routing over ℳ\mathcal{M}. In particular, for cold arms a′∉ℳhota^{\prime}\notin\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{hot}} with a′∉Ca^{\prime}\notin C, hot dominance gives μ⁡(a′,C,x)≤−1−Δdom\mu(a^{\prime};C;x)\leq-1-\Delta_{\mathrm{dom}}, which is far below any cached hot arm, so the margin condition is satisfied a fortiori. ∎

Lemma D.4 (Exploitation play count).

Under 1–2, suppose the bonus condition of Lemma D.3 holds throughout epoch ℓ\ell and the epoch-ℓ\ell cache satisfies Cℓ⊆ℳhotC_{\ell}\subseteq\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{hot}}. Then with probability ≥1−δ′\geq 1-\delta^{\prime}, each a∈ℳhota\in\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{hot}} receives at least pmin⋅2ℓ/2p_{\min}\cdot 2^{\ell}/2 exploitation plays.

Proof.

By Lemma D.3, LinUCB selects aa on every context in XaX_{a} during exploitation. Since contexts are i.i.d., the number of such contexts in 2ℓ2^{\ell} rounds concentrates around pmin⋅2ℓp_{\min}\cdot 2^{\ell}. A Chernoff bound gives at least pmin⋅2ℓ/2p_{\min}\cdot 2^{\ell}/2 with probability ≥1−δ′\geq 1-\delta^{\prime}. ∎

Lemma D.5 (Uniform cache deviation).

Let ε=maxa⁡‖θ^a−θa⋆‖2\varepsilon=\max_{a}\|\hat{\theta}_{a}-\theta_{a}^{\star}\|_{2}, F⁡(S):=𝔼x​[maxa⁡μ⁡(a,S,x)]F(S):=\mathbb{E}_{x}[\max_{a}\mu(a;S;x)], and F^n​(S):=1n​∑t=1nmaxa⁡μ^​(a,S,xt)\hat{F}_{n}(S):=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}\max_{a}\hat{\mu}(a;S;x_{t}). Define ρn:=ε+B¯​2​(K​log⁡(e​N/K)+log⁡(2/δ′))/n\rho_{n}:=\varepsilon+\bar{B}\sqrt{2(K\log(eN/K)+\log(2/\delta^{\prime}))/n}. Then with probability ≥1−δ′\geq 1-\delta^{\prime},

sup|S|≤K|F^n​(S)−F⁡(S)|≤ρn.\sup_{|S|\leq K}|\hat{F}_{n}(S)-F(S)|\leq\rho_{n}.

Consequently, if C^∈arg⁡max|S|≤K​F^n​(S)\hat{C}\in\arg\max_{|S|\leq K}\hat{F}_{n}(S), then for any fixed cache C0C_{0} with |C0|=K|C_{0}|=K, F⁡(C0)−F⁡(C^)≤2​ρnF(C_{0})-F(\hat{C})\leq 2\rho_{n}.

Proof.

Step 1. |maxa⁡μ^​(a,S,x)−maxa⁡μ⁡(a,S,x)|≤ε|\max_{a}\hat{\mu}(a;S;x)-\max_{a}\mu(a;S;x)|\leq\varepsilon for all S,xS,x (pointwise Lipschitz of max).

Step 2. For fixed SS, Yt:=maxa⁡μ⁡(a,S,xt)Y_{t}:=\max_{a}\mu(a;S;x_{t}) are i.i.d. with |Yt|≤B¯|Y_{t}|\leq\bar{B}. By Hoeffding with per-cache failure probability δ0′:=δ′/(e​N/K)K\delta^{\prime}_{0}:=\delta^{\prime}/(eN/K)^{K}, |1n​∑tYt−F⁡(S)|≤B¯​2​log⁡(2/δ0′)/n|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t}Y_{t}-F(S)|\leq\bar{B}\sqrt{2\log(2/\delta^{\prime}_{0})/n}.

Step 3. Union over at most (e​N/K)K(eN/K)^{K} caches of size ≤K\leq K; the total failure probability is at most (e​N/K)K⋅δ0′=δ′(eN/K)^{K}\cdot\delta^{\prime}_{0}=\delta^{\prime}.

Step 4 (uniform deviation). Combining steps 1–3: |F^n​(S)−F⁡(S)|≤ρn|\hat{F}_{n}(S)-F(S)|\leq\rho_{n} for all |S|≤K|S|\leq K.

Step 5 (optimizer gap). F⁡(C0)≤F^n​(C0)+ρn≤F^n​(C^)+ρn≤F⁡(C^)+2​ρnF(C_{0})\leq\hat{F}_{n}(C_{0})+\rho_{n}\leq\hat{F}_{n}(\hat{C})+\rho_{n}\leq F(\hat{C})+2\rho_{n}. ∎

Lemma D.6 (Cache bootstrap).

Under 1–2, there exists ℓcache\ell_{\mathrm{cache}} with Mℓcache>βT2/(σmin​min⁡(Δcache,Δdom)2)M_{\ell_{\mathrm{cache}}}>\beta_{T}^{2}/(\sigma_{\min}\min(\Delta_{\mathrm{cache}},\Delta_{\mathrm{dom}})^{2}) such that for all ℓ≥ℓcache\ell\geq\ell_{\mathrm{cache}}: (i) the algorithm’s cache Cℓ:=arg⁡max|S|=K​F^nℓ+N​mℓ​(S)C_{\ell}:=\arg\max_{|S|=K}\hat{F}_{n_{\ell}+Nm_{\ell}}(S) satisfies Cℓ⊆ℳhotC_{\ell}\subseteq\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{hot}}, and (ii) for every hot cache S⊆ℳhotS\subseteq\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{hot}}, the estimated max maxa⁡μ^​(a,S,x)\max_{a}\hat{\mu}(a;S;x) is achieved by a hot arm (estimated hot dominance), both with high probability.

Proof.

After ℓ+1\ell+1 epochs of forced exploration, every arm a∈ℳa\in\mathcal{M} has ≥Mℓ\geq M_{\ell} plays. By Lemma C.1, ‖θ^a−θa⋆‖Va≤βT\|\hat{\theta}_{a}-\theta_{a}^{\star}\|_{V_{a}}\leq\beta_{T}. By Lemma D.1, λmin​(Va)≥σmin​Mℓ/2\lambda_{\min}(V_{a})\geq\sigma_{\min}M_{\ell}/2. Dividing:

For fixed problem parameters, the switching, forced, and bootstrap terms are all o⁡(T)o(\sqrt{T}), so the leading behavior is 𝒪~​(σ​d​N​T+B¯​K​T)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sigma d\sqrt{NT}+\bar{B}\sqrt{KT}). ∎

Proof summary.

The six terms correspond to routing (Lemma C.2), cache estimation and concentration (Lemma D.5 per epoch), switching (K​γK\gamma per epoch), forced exploration (∑ℓN​mℓ\sum_{\ell}Nm_{\ell} rounds), and bootstrap (2ℓ⋆2^{\ell_{\star}} rounds before bonus and cache conditions hold). Assumption 2 enables the chain: margin →\to correct selection (Lemma D.3), coverage →\to play counts (Lemma D.4), full-dimensionality →\to design matrix growth (Lemma D.7).
